ai.summary: A new Windows infostealer sends the data it steals to an AI model and asks it to rank the victim’s assets by how much money they could bring in, Cisco Talos has found. “There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics,” said Ryan Fetterman, a security researcher at Cisco. The malware calls itself VOLTA-AUTODOXER and turned up through Talos’ CAIRN … More → The post AI-powered infostealer picks out the most profitable parts of your stolen data appeared first on Help Net Security .
ai.title: AI-powered infostealer picks out the most profitable parts of your stolen data

general.summary: A critical Android flaw could allow an attacker to run code on a phone without any user action remotely, Google said in its November security bulletin. The flaw, CVE-2026-58868, affects Android 14 through 17. Phones get the fix with security patch level 2026-11-01 or later, which phone makers and carriers send on their own schedules. As of November 4, Google's bulletin did not report
general.title: Google Issues Patches for Critical Android Flaw That Could Allow RCE Without User Interaction

general.summary: This vulnerability allows remote attackers to create arbitrary files on affected installations of MailEnable. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability. The ZDI has assigned a CVSS rating of 7.4. The following CVEs are assigned: CVE-2026-114556.
general.title: ZDI-26-869: MailEnable Save Directory Traversal Arbitrary File Creation Vulnerability

general.summary: This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Ashlar-Vellum Cobalt. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file. The ZDI has assigned a CVSS rating of 7.8. The following CVEs are assigned: CVE-2026-121744.
general.title: ZDI-26-870: (0Day) Ashlar-Vellum Cobalt XE File Parsing Stack-based Buffer Overflow Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

general.summary: In this Help Net Security interview, Lindsay Kaye, VP of Threat Intelligence at HUMAN Security, talks about what AI-generated malware looks like on the bench. She points to tidy comments, uniform logging messages, and emojis as signs a script came from a model, and notes that decompiled code strips much of that away. Kaye also covers how AI is squeezing the time teams have to patch, where it helps criminals scale fraud, and why her … More → The post What AI-generated malware looks like under the microscope appeared first on Help Net Security .
